doc.title: Walter Booker and Jimmy Cobb interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 30, 1995

title: Advice to audiences: exposure, Nat Adderley's talk, stop-look-listen
summary: Asked for a closing word, they stress exposure, TV, and Nat Adderley's spoken introductions; Booker says 'stop, look and listen'.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Well let me see. I’m trying to figure what I could say, I don’t know what you could say to an audience to do it, but that probably has to be exposure again. You know you’ve got

television now, they probably have to see something on television that they say, well you know I could get into that, or something like that. But I don’t know if you just probably get them and try to take them to a concert, that would probably be, a lot of people couldn’t get there.
Do you, I’m sure you’re familiar with the show that Ramsey Lewis has on T.V.? I like that. I think a lot of people would tune into that and watch that for an hour, you know?
Well I’ll tell you there’s another thing. Nat Adderley has a way that he can rap, and he might get you, he could probably get you interested in it.
Because he’s got that kind of rap you know. So now if he could do that on a major scale or something like that, he might recruit some people.

Yeah. Recruit some people to start listening, or to start playing even. I tell you, I would say in a few words, it might sound a little silly but stop, look and listen. See I have the confidence, we have the confidence that if we are not so busy and if we pay attention, and if we get exposed, and once we listen we get taken. That’s all it would take for playing and listening.

Yeah because you know, some people get exposed and they come to see our band and they don’t know what to expect. And they go away enjoying it. Because Nat has talked them through it, walked them through it like let’s say you know? And like that. So they’ve got a better understanding of it than a band that you just go, some people just come and sit down and hear some guys play and they don’t never say nothing, you know? They don’t even probably call the tunes or something.
It’s really easy to play in Nat’s band.
It’s just hard on a person listening, I mean listening at that. Because they don’t know what they’re listening at. Unless they have an exceptional musical —
Unless they’re already connoisseurs of music.
Probably already have all the albums already, and they’re just hearing it live.

Yeah and what they’re hearing. See the levels change when you already have some predisposed, when you get a little introduction and a little inside comprehension as to what is being done and what the attitude is, and that we’re just human beings too, vulnerable, and quite imperfect as a matter of fact. And it’s about imperfection that makes the magic happen. And that makes everybody know that, before, and the lectures, and the workshops that we have before concerts. By the time we get to the concert we’ll feel good because we know that everybody in there that’s heard that thing, listens and hears and they see things that they would never have seen if it wasn’t for us having a workshop today. You know what I mean?
